clinicalPearls: Presents as firm, tender, deep subcutaneous nodules or plaques favouring the face, upper arms, shoulders, buttocks and thighs, often overlying areas of relative fat abundance
Lesions frequently heal with disfiguring, saucer-like lipoatrophy and depressed scars, a clue to the diagnosis
Overlying skin may be normal or show features of discoid lupus (erythema, follicular plugging, atrophy) when the process is termed lupus profundus
Occurs most often in middle-aged women and may exist in isolation or alongside systemic or discoid lupus erythematosus
Biopsy shows a predominantly lobular lymphocytic panniculitis with lymphoid follicles, hyaline fat necrosis and mucin, often with an overlying interface dermatitis
The main differential of concern is subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma, which can mimic it clinically and histologically
Management centres on antimalarials (hydroxychloroquine) with systemic immunosuppression for resistant disease, plus photoprotection and avoidance of trauma
reference.pathophysiology: Lupus panniculitis is an autoimmune, predominantly lobular inflammation of subcutaneous fat that forms part of the spectrum of cutaneous lupus erythematosus. A T-lymphocyte-driven immune response targets the deep dermis and fat lobules, producing hyaline necrosis of adipocytes, lymphoid aggregates, mucin deposition and lymphocytic vascular injury. Repeated bouts of fat inflammation and necrosis are followed by fibrosis and loss of fat volume, accounting for the characteristic depressed atrophic scars. It may occur alone or in association with discoid or systemic lupus, reflecting a shared loss of immune tolerance.
additionalInvestigations: Deep incisional or excisional biopsy including ample subcutaneous fat for histology
Immunohistochemistry and clonality studies to distinguish from subcutaneous T-cell lymphoma
Antinuclear antibody and extractable nuclear antigen panel
Complement levels, full blood count and inflammatory markers
Assessment for systemic lupus (urinalysis, renal function) where indicated
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging nodules with systemic B-symptoms, cytopenias or haemophagocytosis suggesting lymphoma
Ulceration, extensive necrosis or secondary infection of lesions
Features of active systemic lupus with organ involvement
reference.prognosis: The condition tends to run a chronic, relapsing course; inflammation usually responds to antimalarials but residual lipoatrophy and scarring are frequently permanent and cosmetically distressing. Prognosis worsens if there is coexisting active systemic lupus or if an underlying lymphoma has been mistaken for it.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma as benign lupus panniculitis
Taking a biopsy that is too shallow to sample the fat lobules adequately
Attributing new depressed scars to injections or trauma rather than recognising the panniculitis
Overlooking coexisting systemic lupus and its organ complications
management: Antimalarials such as hydroxychloroquine as first-line disease-modifying therapy for the panniculitis
Systemic or intralesional corticosteroids to control active inflammatory nodules
Escalate refractory disease to methotrexate, mycophenolate, thalidomide, dapsone or rituximab
Strict photoprotection and avoidance of trauma to lesional sites
Exclude subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma histologically before committing to immunosuppression
Monitor for coexisting systemic or discoid lupus with periodic clinical and laboratory review
Defer soft-tissue augmentation for residual lipoatrophy until the disease is quiescent
